summary: A procedural topic: children learn to build and interpret a scale model of the solar system, choosing a scale and applying the same proportion to every planet's size and distance. The headline discovery is that distances between planets are vastly larger than the planets themselves — so large that true sizes and true distances cannot both be shown easily on one convenient scale. The anchor comparison: if the Sun is a beach ball about 30 cm across, Earth is a peppercorn-sized bead (about 3 mm) roughly 32 metres away (about 30 m), and Neptune is about 30 times farther, nearly a kilometre away. The work confronts the textbook image of neatly lined-up, close-together planets, which is not to scale for distance (and often not for size).
misconceptions: Thinking the planets are close together and the solar system is crowded (from textbook diagrams), rather than mostly vast empty space.
Assuming a single scale model can show both true planet sizes and true distances easily — missing that a same-scale model needs an enormous area.
Reading the common 'planets in a neat row, evenly spaced' picture as accurate for size and distance.
Confusing scaling SIZE with scaling DISTANCE — shrinking planets and gaps by different unstated amounts and not noticing.
Believing the outer planets are only a little farther than the inner ones, underestimating how distances balloon toward Neptune.
Thinking a scale model preserves everything (colours, moons, orbits precisely) rather than deliberately representing chosen quantities to a chosen ratio.

activities.title: Pace out a scale solar system (whole-body distance model)
steps: Agree a scale with a concrete anchor: the Sun is a beach ball about 30 cm across; on the same scale Earth is a peppercorn-sized bead about 3 mm across (smaller than a pea).

Using a long tape measure and the run of a field, corridor, or playground, place the Earth-bead at the correct distance on this scale — for a ~30 cm ball this works out to about 32 metres (roughly 30 metres).
Walk out to where each further planet belongs, placing a bead or marker, and keep walking to where Neptune would stand — roughly 30 times farther than Earth, likely off the end of the playground.
Keep the SAME scale for both sizes and distances throughout; measure, don't guess.
Afterwards, compare what you paced out with a textbook 'planets in a neat row' picture and decide whether that picture is to scale.
activities.insight: The planets are tiny specks separated by huge, mostly empty gaps; the distances dwarf the planet sizes, and one consistent scale forces you to spread the model over a very large space.

activities.title: Choose a scale and apply the proportion
steps: Pick the Sun's model size (e.g. a ball of a chosen diameter) as the scale anchor.
Use the proportion scale size ÷ real size = scale distance ÷ real distance to work out each planet's scaled size and scaled distance from the same ratio.
Build (or set up on a build-and-scroll tool) a SIZE model and a separate DISTANCE model, and try to combine them on one scale.
Record how long the combined model would have to be for both to be shown together.
Check your anchor facts: a 30 cm beach-ball Sun gives a peppercorn-sized Earth (about 3 mm) roughly 32 metres away; Neptune, about 4.5 billion km out, lands about 30 times farther (nearly 1 km).
activities.insight: A single scale applied consistently to sizes and distances cannot show both comfortably on one convenient layout — a true combined model needs an enormous space (e.g. with a 1-cm Earth, the Sun is about 1.1 m across and Neptune is about 3.5 km, over two miles, away; the length depends on the scale chosen). You choose which quantity a model represents.

activities.title: Travel the gaps on screen (digital build-and-scroll or flight)
steps: On a build-your-own-scale-model tool, set the Sun's size and let the tool place all planets to that scale.
Flip between a SIZE-scale view and a DISTANCE-scale view and note why they can't coexist comfortably on one page.
Pan or scroll to 'travel' from the Sun outward — past mostly empty black — to reach Earth, then keep going to Neptune; use a distance/time or length readout to register the emptiness.
Apply a 'is this to scale?' check to the neat lined-up textbook row and mark whether it is accurate for distance and size.
activities.insight: Even on screen, traversing the gaps shows the planets are tiny and the space between them is enormous; the lined-up textbook picture is not to scale.

activities.title: Check and read scale models (interpretation practice)
steps: Given a labelled scale diagram, tap or look up the scaled size and distance of each planet and state the anchor facts (30 cm beach-ball Sun → peppercorn-sized Earth, about 3 mm, roughly 32 m away).
Compare which is bigger: a planet, or the gap to the next planet.
Decide whether a given diagram is to scale for size, for distance, for both, or for neither, and justify your answer.
Sequence the planets by distance and estimate, e.g. where Earth sits if the Sun were a beach ball.
Explain what a scale model does and does not preserve (it shows chosen quantities to a chosen ratio, not necessarily colours, moons, or exact orbits).
activities.insight: Reading a scale model means knowing what quantity it represents and at what ratio — and that most diagrams compress distance to fit a page.

checkQuestion: Give the child a working scale: the Sun is a beach ball about 30 cm across. Hand them a pea for Earth, a small bead for Neptune, a long tape measure, and the run of the playground. Set the task: 'Place the Earth-pea at the right distance from the Sun on THIS scale, then go and stand where Neptune would be.' Watch what they DO — do they keep the SAME scale for sizes and distances, and do they end up walking tens of metres out for Earth (and far off the playground for Neptune), rather than bunching the planets a few steps from the Sun?
checkAnswer: A correct performance applies one consistent scale: with the Sun as a ~30 cm beach ball, the Earth-pea is placed about 25–30 metres away, and Neptune ends up roughly 30 times farther still — hundreds of metres away, likely off the end of the playground. The child treats the planets as tiny specks separated by huge, mostly empty gaps, and does NOT shrink the distances to keep the planets near the Sun. The size-scale and the distance-scale stay the same throughout.
